In this episode
OpenCode is one of the fastest-growing AI developer tools around, surging in just a few months from roughly 650,000 monthly active users to nearly 8 million, and almost 1M daily active users.
In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, we meet Dax Raad, co-founder of OpenCode, for a discussion about the gaps in developer tooling that led him to build OpenCode, the advantages of open source, and why taste and engineering judgment matter even more as AI becomes a core part of software development.
We also cover how OpenCode turned Anthropic’s blocking of integration with Claude Code into a massive growth lever by partnering with OpenAI and other model providers, why GPU demand is becoming a bottleneck everywhere, how come AI coding tools don’t automatically mean engineering teams move faster, and also why Dax is personally skeptical about predictions for the future of engineering and work, in general.
I found this conversation especially interesting because Dax displays a healthy skepticism toward the benefits of AI, even while building one of the most popular AI coding harnesses.
My observations from the conversation with Dax
Here are 14 of my most interesting takeaways from talking with Dax:
1. AI makes coding easier, but the hard parts of the job don’t vanish. Dax remarks that a lot of the job has become objectively easier with AI, but then follows up with a simple question: why does it feel like he is still having to think as hard as he ever did?
2. Thinking upfront beats building prototypes and seeing what sticks. This is especially true in the period before a product-market fit is found, Dax says. AI doesn’t help much in this early phase because the problem is figuring out what to build, not how fast you can build it, he says. Therefore, thinking hard about the right direction for development beats taking unfocused swings at different ideas.
3. Shipping 10x more features is a recipe for a Frankenstein-like product. It’s tempting to one-to-one prompt an agent for every user’s complaint or competitor’s feature. But the more features are jammed into a product, the worse it tends to become. Also, don’t forget that every shipped feature will need to be supported for as long as it’s part of the product!
4. No AI-native coding agent company is “winning” by being better with AI. Dax says that none of OpenCode’s competitors are crushing them, and that nobody is using AI so well that others cannot compete.
5. For OpenCode, product positioning beats speed of execution. A massive reason for OpenCode becoming the most popular open source AI coding harness is that they noticed no coding agent had successfully claimed the open source category. Dax was wondering why not, given that every market-leading dev tool across the industry is open source. So, he and the team focused on positioning and it paid off handsomely. He summarizes: “Get positioning right and the world just keeps handing you wins you didn’t expect.”
6. OpenCode’s “inverted” strategy: start with a good-enough product, then optimize. Dax admits their harness wasn’t ideal during OpenCode’s first five months, but it was still good enough. “Once we won enough market share, we went back and tried to make our harness good and smart.”
7. Most software engineers profit from AI as time gained, not increased output — unless you change incentives! Dax says the natural way for software engineers to “cash out” their AI tooling gains is with time savings, by doing the same work as before, but faster. Until compensation and motivation structures change, most teams should expect output to stay flat while engineers go home earlier. There’s nothing wrong with this, but AI vendors sell a different outcome to CFOs: increased output.
8. Motivated engineers who care about quality get buried by slop PRs from devs who don’t care. Dax has hired people from companies where they were one of the few who still cared about quality. In contrast, former colleagues just pumped out AI-generated code and focused on getting their tasks done, ignorant of the decreasing quality of code. Motivated devs feel they are drowning in garbage code and tech debt, and getting burnt out by trying to clean it up. Dax calls this an engineering leadership problem that most companies don’t notice.
9. AI code generation mutes the “guilt” of doing the wrong thing, but this builds up tech debt. Pre-AI, writing a hack felt bad, the second time it felt really bad, and by the third time you’d often just refactor in order to fix up the code. Now, the agent hides the hack, which skews devs’ judgment and results in less tech debt being cleaned up.
10. Dealing with tech debt is easier than ever, and teams should do more of it. Agents make refactoring across a codebase cheap: for example, ask an agent to implement a new pattern everywhere across the codebase. It’s very easy and cheap to clear up tech debt, today. So, do more of it!
11. AI has not really changed the thinking / doing ratio for Dax. “Pre-AI, I would spend 95% of my energy thinking about what to do and 5% on doing it. Now I spend 96% of my time thinking, and 4% on actually doing it. So, it’s like a 20% improvement [from 5% doing to 4% doing], but day to day, it feels as hard as ever.”
12. Confident predictions about AI are often forms of self-reassurance. A post went viral on X claiming that 24-29 year-old engineers will dominate in the future, which was written by – you can guess – someone in that exact age bracket. --------------------------------------------------

**Second, by tapping unexpected investors. **Wesley Wang Media is funded by a suite of mostly tech investors. Through cold emails and attending events, Wang raised $250K from individual investors. Now, his total fundraising across the production co. and individual projects has topped $1M.

## 🔥==** Lead Story**==

**[Google Ads Expands AI Max to Shopping and Travel](https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/ai-max-new-features/)**

==Google rolled out the next chapter of AI Max, one year after launch.==

==AI Max is now expanding into Shopping campaigns and travel-specific ad formats, a new "AI Brief" tool lets advertisers guide messaging and audience targeting, and Final URL expansion now supports mandatory text disclaimers for regulated industries.==

==That last one matters more than it sounds. Until now, FUE was off-limits for anyone in finance, health, or legal because compliance text couldn't be guaranteed. Shopping advertisers can no longer treat AI Max as a Search-only conversation. ==

==If you run an e-commerce or travel business, your bidding logic and asset library are about to be evaluated differently. Pull a Shopping campaign and check whether AI Max eligibility is now active in your account. ==

==Run one test campaign with AI Brief inputs before you migrate the budget.==

## 📰==** Breaking News**==

**[IAB Tech Lab Publishes AI Bot Management Guidance](https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/415340/iab-opens-ai-bot-guidance-for-new-web-rules.html)**

==The IAB Tech Lab released new guidance covering how publishers and content owners should approach AI crawlers and non-human traffic.==

==The CoMP Working Group laid out the tradeoffs across bot-management strategies, from full blocks to commercial agreements via the CoMP API.==

==This is the operational layer that follows the technical CoMP v1.0 spec. The IAB's own research shows publishers facing 30-60% traffic declines from AI-driven zero-click search, so the urgency is real.==

==If you own a content site or run content marketing for a brand, your robots.txt is now a revenue decision, not an IT setting. Audit your current bot policy this week.==

**[Reddit Brings Max Campaigns and Dual Attribution to App Advertisers](https://dcrayons.app/insights/reddit-app-ads-get-smarter-max-campaigns-aeo-dual-attribution-explained)**

==Reddit rolled out updates, extending its automated Max campaign format to app advertisers and launching Dual Attribution in beta.==

==It's a new system that combines Reddit first-party data with MMP and SKAdNetwork last-touch reporting inside Ads Manager.==

==Reddit says Max campaigns delivered an avg 15% CPA reduction in early app testing, and install volume from app campaigns is up 129% YOY.==

==If you run app install campaigns, Reddit just became measurable enough to compare against Meta and TikTok on the same dashboard. Request Dual Attribution beta access through your Reddit rep if app installs are part of your stack.==

## ==**📚 Strategy Piece**==

==**["Marketing Teams Already Missed the AI Window" - Ryan Warren](https://martech.org/ai-wont-save-a-broken-organization/)**==

==Razorfish's Chief CRM Officer argues that most marketing teams had a chance to use AI to rebuild how they work, and instead used it to do the same mediocre work faster.==

==He says to stop using AI to scale the send cannon. Use it to rebuild the operating model around trust, identity, and connected experiences.==

==It's a tidy thesis from someone selling agency services for exactly this transformation. Most in-house teams don't have the runway to "rebuild from the ground up." ==

==They are the ones who deleted half of it and rebuilt with smaller, sharper signals. If your AI workflow is just "write the same email faster," you are proving his point.==

## @benradack
The first 30 days of a new client account. What I do, what I don't touch, and why.

**Week 1: Stop the bleeding**

→ Audit the account but don't make major structural changes yet
→ Turn off ads that have been running 2+ weeks with zero results
→ Pull historical winners back into a fresh CBO with a cost cap
→ Launch a batch test in the ABO with whatever creative the client has on hand

The goal isn't to fix everything. The goal is to find quick wins and stop the account from getting worse.

**Week 2: Build the foundation**

→ Restructure the account based on spend level (under $1k/day = consolidated, over $1k/day = separated testing and scaling)
→ Set up custom columns and audience segments properly
→ Start a real testing pipeline with one angle per ad set
→ Launch a zombie campaign for the failed ads from week 1

**Week 3: Find the winners**

→ Heavy creative testing. As many new angles as the client's creative team can produce.
→ Daily breakdowns on everything from week 1 to see what's actually working
→ Graduate any proven testing winners into the scaling CBO
→ Start dialing in cost caps on scaling based on real data

**Week 4: Optimize and document**

→ Refine the structure based on what's working
→ Document the wins and the patterns I'm seeing
→ Build the creative brief for month 2 based on what tested well
→ Set the testing cadence going forward

## @benradack
Take your top 10 Instagram posts from the last 90 days.
Drop them into an ABO testing campaign. One post per ad set.

Use the same post IDs. All the existing engagement carries over with the ad. Likes, comments, shares. Meta sees a post people already responded to and wants to push it.

Run it like any other testing campaign.

→ Watch link CTR and ATC rate first 
→ CPA and ROAS second 
→ Give each post a real chance with proper spend before judging

When one starts performing, duplicate it to your scaling CBO.

These often outperform polished ad creative because they don't look like ads. They look like content. The audience that scrolled past your ad version stops on the same idea coming through as a regular post.

Plus Meta tends to favor them in scaling because they already have social proof baked in.

If you're not running your top organic posts as ads, you're leaving free performance on the table.

1. "I understand my problem better than I did before."

This is the mechanism section.

The reader learns something specific about why their problem exists.
Not a symptom -> a cause.

2. "The things I've tried weren't wrong, they just weren't addressing the actual issue."

This is the failed solutions + root cause.

It removes guilt and creates openness to something new.

3. "This solution makes logical sense given what I just learned."

This is the CTA.
The product isn't sold.
It's the inevitable conclusion of the argument the advertorial just made.

If your advertorial isn't creating all three, the CTA is doing all the heavy lifting.

And CTAs aren't built for that.

## @oliverwhudson
A lot of brands we come across are working against two forces: one they cant control and one they can

The first is CPM inflation. Since 2021 the cost to reach a thousand people on Meta has increased around 50 to 60%. More advertisers, same supply. It's structural and it compounds yoy

The second is audience quality degradation. The first customers you acquire are the easiest, but as you spend more you move further from that golden cohort. Broader audiences, more resistance, lower conversion rates. The further you scale, the harder each incremental acquisition becomes

Multiply those two together and you're looking at a natural CAC increase of roughly 20% every year just from scaling. If your growth target is 20%, you need to improve by around 42% net just to stay still

Brands try to solve this entirely through creative and media buying.. and great creative buys you time but there's a ceiling to what that can do alone

The two levers that extend the ceiling are offer architecture and post-click conversion

Offer architecture: increasing the perceived value of what you're selling so you can afford a higher CAC and still be profitable. More ads clear the efficiency threshold, more ads become winners, the hit rate on your creative inventory goes up

Post click conversion: making the funnel work harder so the traffic you've already paid for converts at a higher rate. Every percentage point improvement in conversion rate is free spend efficiency

Gets turned off.

The Zombie Campaign rule is that any creative that died with directional signal gets resurrected within 60 days with a different setup.

What counts as directional signal:

1. CTR above account average even if CPA missed
2. Hook hold rate strong but click-through weak
3. Strong engagement on a specific demographic segment
4. Comments or shares that show the angle hit emotionally

Take a creative that hit any one of those and rebuild around it. New landing page. New audience temperature.

> Different placement priority
> Run it again with the variable changed

We've had creatives that died on round one come back as top performers six weeks later. Because the setup around it changed (not the creative).

How email marketing will soon change for the better:
- Testing layered on good strategy: instead of designing 1 welcome email, you design 10 in the same amount of time each testing something specific
- Cohort segmentation: one campaign turns into 10, each targeting users at different LTV stages. E.g. A promo looks different to someone in first 10 days vs. someone who bought 180 days ago vs. someone who never purchased.
- Smarter link tracking and insights. E.g. customers click x times before purchase, customers who clicked this email were X times more likely to purchase, etc. This kinda exists, but AI will enable us to sift through the endless data and identify what matters and what is BS. More powerful flows will evolve from this.

The biggest brands will benefit most from AI acceleration in email. They have the most data and ability to test, but often even they can't escape the need for statistical significance.

Leveraging this tech in 80/20 situations is what will bring outsized returns. I.e. slicing up your winback flow 30 ways won't, while testing 10 different welcome journey could unlock meaningful CVR wins.
